sounds.name: First Drone
sounds.ref: Classic technique: five saws tuned into a chord
sounds.blurb: One classic drone voice: five saws tuned by ear into a C major chord.
sounds.how: A classic drone voice has no volt-per-octave: five sawtooth generators, each tuned by its own knob, sound together while the voice is open. Its DRONE VOICES button latches it open; here the keyboard’s gate opens it instead, so it plays when you do. Tune the five into a chord, then play VCO A over it.

steps.title: Open Drone 1
steps.why:
The keys play VCO A, so this lesson turns its channel down first, to hear the drone alone.
- VCO A VOL 0.
- Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE: Drone 1 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it. RELEASE 8, so it rides over the gaps between notes.
- Listen for: a dense cluster while a key is held, five saws at the middle of their ranges.

steps.title: Tune the low pair
steps.why:
Generators 1 and 2 are the low ones. Tune 1 to C2 and 2 to G2, a fifth above.
- Listen for: the bottom of the cluster settling into an open fifth.

steps.title: Tune the top three
steps.why:
Generator 3 to E3, 4 to C5 and 5 to G5: a spread C major chord across five octaves.
- Listen for: the beating stop as each one lands. Tuning by ear is the instrument: the manual warns the generators drift and need touching up.

steps.title: Mute two generators
steps.why:
MUTE switches a generator out; its lamp in the OSC STATUS bar goes dark.
- MUTE 4 and 5 off.
- Listen for: the chord closing down to a low triad.

steps.title: Play a line over it
steps.why:
VCO A’s VOL up to 5, WAVEFORM to triangle, Envelope A ATTACK 3, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 6. The keys play VCO A on top; the drone follows them only in time, since its pitch is set on its own knobs.
- Listen for: a soft melody in the drone’s key.

context.d1.tune1: In this sound: C2, the root.
context.d1.on4: In this sound: off, for a low triad.

tweaks.try: Move TUNE 3 slowly either side of E3
tweaks.hear: Beating against the other generators, faster the further it goes, until it lands on another interval.

tweaks.try: Turn RLS up and press DRONE VOICES 1 off
tweaks.hear: The chord dies away slowly instead of stopping.

sounds.name: Falling Chord
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a drone chord bent by its own envelope
sounds.blurb: An A minor chord struck on each key that slides down a fifth to D minor as it fades.
sounds.how: A classic drone’s envelope comes out at its env jack, and its CV jack bends every generator whose MOD is on by the same interval. Patch the one into the other and the chord is bent up while the voice is open and sinks back as it fades: struck as A minor, it falls a fifth and lands on D minor. Every generator moves by the same amount, so the chord stays in tune all the way down. The keyboard’s gate opens the drone, so each key strikes the chord again.

steps.title: Tune D minor
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0, so only the drone sounds. Drone 2 tuned to D1, A2, D3, F4, A5: D minor, wide open. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 2’s GATE, so each key opens it.
- Listen for: a dark minor chord on each key.

steps.title: Let the envelope bend it
steps.why:
All five MOD buttons on, the CV knob to 7.3, and patch Drone 2’s env out to its own CV jack. While the voice is open the envelope bends every generator up a fifth.
- Listen for: the chord now sounding as A minor while the key is held.

steps.title: A long fall
steps.why:
ATT 3 for a soft strike, RLS 8 for a long fade.
- Listen for: the chord sliding down a fifth as it fades after each key.

steps.title: Soften and widen it
steps.why:
Both filters’ FREQ to 5, and CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 3 (Space reverb), BLEND 4.
- Listen for: the saws rounded off, and the fall trailing into the room.

context.d2.cv: In this sound: 7.3, just enough for the envelope to bend the chord a fifth.

tweaks.hear: A slower, longer fall.
A smaller fall, about a fourth, landing on a different chord.

sounds.name: Cross-Mod Metal
sounds.ref: Classic technique: oscillators modulating each other
sounds.blurb: VOLT past half way: the five saws frequency-modulate each other into a metallic roar.
sounds.how: After half its turn VOLT stops just lowering the generators and starts them modulating each other, which the manual calls an FM synthesis effect. The chord turns rough, clangorous and alive. A resonant filter on top picks out a moving whistle. With the keyboard’s gate opening it, short notes strike the roar like a gong.

steps.title: Open Drone 4
steps.why:
The keys play VCO A, so this lesson turns its channel down first, to hear the drone alone.
- VCO A VOL 0, Drone 4 centred.
- Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 4’s GATE: Drone 4 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it.
- Listen for: a short burst of the cluster on each key.

steps.title: Turn VOLT past half way
steps.why:
VOLT 8.
- Listen for: the chord dropping, then breaking up into a rough, metallic growl as the generators modulate each other.

steps.title: Resonate the filters
steps.why:
Both filters' FREQ to 4.5 and RES to 7.
- Listen for: a whistling peak riding on the growl.

context.d4.volt: In this sound: 8, well into the cross-modulation.

tweaks.hear: The sound tipping from a falling chord into metal and back.
The roar thins: the cross-modulation runs through every generator that is in.

sounds.name: Photosensor Wobble
sounds.ref: Classic technique: an LFO bending a drone’s pitch
sounds.blurb: LFO A lights a drone's photosensor, so the generators with MOD on waver in pitch.
sounds.how: Each classic drone has a photosensor, the eye, that bends the generators whose MOD button is on. On the hardware the room's light moves it too. Its CV jack lights a red LED in front of it, which is why the LFOs swing positive only: patch LFO A in and the chosen generators drift up and back while the others hold.

steps.title: Open Drone 1 on a chord
steps.why:
The keys play VCO A, so this lesson turns its channel down first, to hear the drone alone.
- VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1 tuned to D minor: D2, A2, F3, D5, A5.
- Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE: Drone 1 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it. RELEASE 8.

steps.title: Light the eye with LFO A
steps.why:
Patch LFO A's out to Drone 1's CV jack, and set the LFO slow and smooth: RATE 3, WAVE at triangle.
- Listen for: nothing yet. No generator has MOD on, so the light does nothing.

steps.title: Turn MOD on for the top two
steps.why:
MOD 4 and 5 on, and CV 4.
- Listen for: the top of the chord sighing up and back with the LFO while the bass stays put.

steps.title: Play a line over it
steps.why:
VCO A’s VOL up to 5, WAVEFORM to triangle, Envelope A ATTACK 3, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 6. The keys play VCO A on top; the drone follows them only in time, since its pitch is set on its own knobs. Its notes overlap, so the line is legato and the drone never closes.
- Listen for: a soft melody in the drone’s key.

context.d1.mod4: In this sound: on, so the LFO bends generator 4.
context.d1.cv: In this sound: how far the LFO bends.

tweaks.hear: The bass joins the wobble, and the chord loses its anchor.
The bent notes jump between two pitches instead of gliding.

sounds.name: Papa Srapa Siren
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a square wave swept by a slow modulator
sounds.blurb: A square tone swung up and down by its own slow square: a siren.
sounds.how: The Papa Srapa voices are two square oscillators: a slow one, the modulator, and a tone. With FM on the modulator throws the tone between two pitches, and MOD and DIVIDER set how far apart. Slow it down and it is a siren. Unlike a classic drone, a Papa Srapa voice has a pitch input, so the keyboard can play the siren.

steps.title: Open Drone 3
steps.why:
The keys play VCO A, so this lesson turns its channel down first, to hear the drone alone.
- VCO A VOL 0, Drone 3 centred.
- Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 3’s GATE: Drone 3 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it. And patch the keyboard’s v/oct out to Drone 3’s cv: the Papa Srapa’s tone follows the keys, PITCH setting where middle C lands.
- Listen for: a plain buzzy square that moves with the keys.

steps.title: Turn FM on
steps.why:
FM on: the modulator now moves the tone. MOD 5 sets how far.
- Listen for: a two-note see-saw.

steps.title: Slow it to a siren
steps.why:
RATE 2.
- Listen for: the two pitches alternating at a siren's pace.

steps.title: Soften the edges
steps.why:
Both filters' FREQ to 5.5.
- Listen for: a rounder, more distant siren.

context.d3.mod: In this sound: the interval between the two pitches.

tweaks.hear: The two pitches close in until it is a trill.
The see-saw speeds up into a rough, ringing buzz.

sounds.name: Space Birds
sounds.ref: Classic technique: fast, chirping frequency modulation
sounds.blurb: FM and AM together on a high tone: chirps that the TIME cartridge echoes into a flock.
sounds.how: With both FM and AM on, the modulator moves the tone and chops it at once: one pitch is sounded, the other silenced, so each pulse is a short chirp. A high range and a quick rate make birdsong, and a delay cartridge throws the chirps across the stereo field. The keyboard plays it through the voice’s gate and pitch inputs: short notes are single calls.

steps.title: Open Drone 6 high
steps.why:
The keys play VCO A, so this lesson turns its channel down first, to hear the drone alone.
- VCO A VOL 0. Drone 6 HI / LOW on, PITCH 6, VOL 8, RELEASE 6 so each call trails off.
- Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 6’s GATE: Drone 6 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it. And patch the keyboard’s v/oct out to Drone 6’s cv, so the keys set each call’s pitch.
- Listen for: a high square on each key.

steps.title: FM and AM together
steps.why:
FM on and AM on, MOD 6, RATE 7.
- Listen for: rapid chirps, each one a jump in pitch cut short.

steps.title: Load the TIME cartridge
steps.why:
Load TIME on both sides, program 1 (delay and reverb): Y sets the delay time, X the feedback. BLEND 5.
- Listen for: the chirps echoing back from both sides.

context.d6.am: In this sound: on, so every other half of the modulator is silent.

tweaks.hear: The chirps blur into a buzzing insect.
Longer gaps before the echoes, a bigger space.

sounds.name: Surf
sounds.ref: Classic technique: filtered noise as the sea
sounds.blurb: A Papa Srapa voice as pure noise, its filter swept by a slow LFO: waves on a beach.
sounds.how: The manual's recipe for clean noise: FM and AM off, PITCH at zero, MOD and DIVIDER at maximum, NOISE at maximum. A slow LFO into the filter's CV then makes the noise swell and fall like surf. The keyboard’s gate opens the voice, so each held note is one wave.

steps.title: Drone 3 as clean noise
steps.why:
The keys play VCO A, so this lesson turns its channel down first, to hear the drone alone.
- VCO A VOL 0, Drone 3 centred. PITCH 0, MOD 10, DIVIDER 10, NOISE 10, as the manual says.
- Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 3’s GATE: Drone 3 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it. ATTACK 7 and RELEASE 8, so each key is a wave that builds and draws back.
- Listen for: hiss that swells on each key.

steps.title: Close the filters
steps.why:
FREQ 4 on both sides, RES 3.
- Listen for: a dull roar.

steps.title: Let the LFO open them
steps.why:
Patch LFO A into CV L. With nothing in CV R it moves both filters. RATE 2.5, WAVE at triangle, MOD L 7.
- Listen for: the roar swelling and falling back every few seconds.

context.vcf.lmod: In this sound: how far each wave rises.

tweaks.hear: Longer, slower waves.
The left side thins to a whistling wind.

sounds.name: Lead Over the Drone
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a melody over a held drone
sounds.blurb: A drone chord from Drone 1 under a VCO A melody, both in the Cathedral cartridge.
sounds.how: The manual’s point is that the SOLAR makes a whole piece without multitrack recording: drones hold the harmony while the touch keyboard plays VCO A on top. Here Drone 1 holds C minor, opened by the keyboard’s gate so it comes and goes with the line, and VCO A plays a slow melody, the two in one reverb.

steps.title: The drone underneath
steps.why:
Drone 1 tuned to C minor: C2, G2, E♭3, C5, G5, its VOL down to 5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE: Drone 1 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it. RELEASE 8, so it holds across the line.
- Listen for: a dark chord under each note.

steps.title: Shape VCO A
steps.why:
VCO A plays the melody. Envelope A: ATTACK 3, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 6, for a soft, singing note.
- Listen for: the line swelling in over the chord.

steps.title: Round the wave
steps.why:
WAVEFORM to triangle.
- Listen for: a flute-like line.

steps.title: Into the Cathedral
steps.why:
Load CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1 (Shimmer): Z sets the reverb's decay. BLEND 6.
- Listen for: everything in one big space.

context.va.wave: In this sound: triangle, soft against the saws.

tweaks.hear: The line gains a square an octave below, more body.
A shorter reverb and a closer, drier line.

sounds.name: Sub Bass
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a sub-oscillator bass
sounds.blurb: VCO A three octaves down with its sub-oscillator, under a closed filter.
sounds.how: The 42N's VCOs gained a −1 SUB switch: a square an octave below whatever wave is chosen. With the OCT +3 / LOW switch at LOW and the filter closed, VCO A is a deep, round bass.

steps.title: Drop VCO A three octaves
steps.why:
OCT +3 / LOW to LOW.
- Listen for: the saw falling to a buzzy bass.

steps.title: A square and its sub
steps.why:
WAVEFORM to square and −1 SUB on.
- Listen for: a hollow bass with a deeper octave under it.

steps.title: Close the filters
steps.why:
FREQ 4 on both sides.
- Listen for: the buzz gone, the weight left.

steps.title: Make it punch
steps.why:
Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 4, SUSTAIN 5, RELEASE 2.
- Listen for: a firm start to each note.

context.va.sub: In this sound: on, the octave below.

tweaks.hear: The square narrows to a thinner, nasal pulse.
A rubbery peak on the left side.

sounds.name: FM Bell
sounds.ref: Classic technique: two-oscillator FM bells
sounds.blurb: VCO A frequency-modulating VCO B through the normal into its CV input: struck bells.
sounds.how: VCO A is wired inside to VCO B's CV input, and VCO B's CV AMT sets how far it moves VCO B's pitch: frequency modulation with no cable. Hear only VCO B, tune VCO A against it and give VCO B a struck envelope, and the keys play bells.

steps.title: Hear VCO B alone
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0 and VCO B VOL 7. VCO A still runs, feeding VCO B.
- Listen for: VCO B's saw on the keys.

steps.title: Two sines
steps.why:
Both VCOs to sine, and VCO A's TUNE to 9 so it sits off VCO B's pitch.
- Listen for: a pure tone.

steps.title: Turn the FM up
steps.why:
VCO B's CV AMT 4: VCO A now frequency-modulates it.
- Listen for: the sine turning into a bright, inharmonic bell.

steps.title: Strike it
steps.why:
Envelope B: ATTACK 0, DECAY 8, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 7.
- Listen for: each note struck and ringing away.

context.vb.cvamt: In this sound: how bright the bell is.
context.va.tune: In this sound: sets which bell, by the ratio of the two pitches.

tweaks.hear: The bell's colour changing, harmonic at some points, clangorous between.
A harsher, brighter strike.

sounds.name: Night Sequence
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a five-step analogue sequence
sounds.blurb: Each key steps the 5-step sequencer on and sets its key, playing a minor figure on VCO A over a low drone.
sounds.how: The sequencer is a Buchla-style voltage source: five knobs, five gate switches and a clock. Its cv out into VCO A’s 1v/oct adds each step to the key you hold, half a volt a knob unit, so six semitones a unit. Clocked from the keyboard’s gate instead of the PULSER, each key you press moves it on one step, so the keyboard plays the figure and moves it to a new key. A soft filter, a long release and the Cathedral turn it into a melody, and Drone 1 holds the root and fifth underneath.

steps.title: Patch the sequencer to VCO A
steps.why:
Patch cv out to VCO A’s 1v/oct and VCO A’s VOL up to 9. The steps start on a minor figure: 0, 3, 7, 5 and 10 semitones above the key you hold.
- Listen for: the notes jumping as the PULSER steps on its own.

steps.title: Clock it from the keys
steps.why:
Patch the keyboard’s gate out to the sequencer’s clock in: it takes over from the PULSER, so each key you press steps the sequence on once.
- Listen for: one step of the figure on each note, in the key you play.

steps.title: Soften the notes
steps.why:
Envelope A: ATTACK 2, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 3, RELEASE 8, so each note blooms and rings into the next.
- Listen for: notes that overlap instead of stopping.

steps.title: Round the wave and the filter
steps.why:
VCO A to triangle, and both filters’ FREQ down to 5 with RES 4: the buzz goes, and a soft peak sings on each note.
- Listen for: a mellow, glassy tone.

steps.title: A drone underneath
steps.why:
Drone 1, generators 1 and 2 only, tuned to C2, G2: the root and fifth, VOL 5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE: Drone 1 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it. RELEASE 9, so it holds between notes.
- Listen for: a low bed the melody moves over.

steps.title: Into the Cathedral
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1 (Shimmer), Z 7 for a long decay, BLEND 6.
- Listen for: the notes hanging in a large space.

context.seq.s3: In this sound: 1.17, seven semitones up.
context.ea.r: In this sound: 8, so each note rings into the next.

tweaks.hear: Only the first three notes, a shorter, rocking figure.
The top note rises from the seventh to the octave.

sounds.name: Open Fifths
sounds.ref: In the style of drone music built on open fifths, after the organum of medieval church music
sounds.blurb: One drone tuned in stacked fifths on D, softened and spread by the TIME cartridge’s chorus.
sounds.how: Fifths are the oldest drone there is: no third, so neither major nor minor, and every generator rings with the others. Drone 2’s five generators span four octaves here, from D2 up to E6, and the TIME cartridge’s delay chorus thickens them into something like a choir or a hurdy-gurdy. The keyboard’s gate opens it, and VCO A plays a modal line over it.

steps.title: Stack the fifths
steps.why:
Drone 2 tuned to D2, A2, E3, A4, E6: D and A, with E above, a fifth on a fifth. VOL 8. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 2’s GATE: Drone 2 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it.
- Listen for: a hollow, ringing chord with no major or minor in it.

steps.title: A slow swell
steps.why:
Drone 2’s ATTACK 6 and RELEASE 8.
- Listen for: the chord arriving like a breath, and fading slowly when it stops.

steps.title: Soften it
steps.why:
Both filters’ FREQ to 5 and RES 2.
- Listen for: the top fifths sweeter, less buzzy.

steps.title: A chorus around it
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 2 (Delay chorus), BLEND 6.
- Listen for: the chord thickening and moving, as if several players held it.

steps.title: Play a line over it
steps.why:
VCO A’s VOL up to 5, WAVEFORM to triangle, Envelope A ATTACK 3, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 6. The keys play VCO A on top; the drone follows them only in time, since its pitch is set on its own knobs. Its notes overlap, so the line runs on like a hurdy-gurdy’s.
- Listen for: a soft melody in the drone’s key.

context.d2.tune3: In this sound: E3, the fifth above the A.

tweaks.hear: Plain octaves and fifths: barer and darker.
The fifths sag apart and start to growl as the generators cross-modulate.

sounds.name: Dusk Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s ambient drone records
sounds.blurb: Two drones hold an F major ninth, a hair apart left and right, breathing through slow filters.
sounds.how: A classic drone’s five generators can be tuned to any chord, so two of them make a wide pad. Drone 1 on the left and Drone 4 on the right hold the same voicing, Drone 4 tuned a hair sharp so the two beat slowly against each other. LFO A into CV L moves both filters through the normal to CV R, each side by its own MOD, so the two sides breathe at different depths. The keyboard’s gate opens both, and VCO A plays a slow line on top.

steps.title: Tune the chord
steps.why:
Drone 1 tuned to F2, C3, A3, E4, G5: F major with the seventh and ninth on top. ATTACK 7 and RELEASE 8 so it swells in and fades out. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE: Drone 1 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it.
- Listen for: a bright, open chord.

steps.title: A second drone, a hair sharp
steps.why:
Drone 4, the same chord with each TUNE a touch higher, also opened by the keyboard’s gate. PAN Drone 1 hard left and Drone 4 hard right, both at VOL 7.
- Listen for: a slow shimmer as the two sides drift against each other.

steps.title: Darken the filters
steps.why:
Both filters’ FREQ down to 4, RES 3.
- Listen for: the saws’ edge gone, a warm chord left.

steps.title: Let them breathe
steps.why:
Patch LFO A to CV L, RATE 3 (one breath every ten seconds or so) its WAVE at triangle. Nothing is in CV R, so CV L moves the right filter too: MOD L 1.5, MOD R 2.5.
- Listen for: the chord slowly opening and closing, further on the right.

steps.title: Into the Cathedral
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1 (Shimmer), Z 8, BLEND 5.
- Listen for: a pad with no edges.

steps.title: Play a line over it
steps.why:
VCO A’s VOL up to 4, WAVEFORM to triangle, Envelope A ATTACK 3, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 6. The keys play VCO A on top; the drone follows them only in time, since its pitch is set on its own knobs. Its notes overlap, so the pad never closes while you play.
- Listen for: a soft melody in the drone’s key.

context.mix.d4.pan: In this sound: hard right, against Drone 1 hard left.

sounds.name: Drone Choir
sounds.ref: In the style of the vocal drones of 1970s and 1980s ambient records
sounds.blurb: A minor chord split over two drones and sung through two band-pass filters, one vowel each side.
sounds.how: The Polivoks filter’s band-pass makes a single peak, and a peak in the right place sounds like a vowel. Each side of the 42N has its own filter, so the two drones can sing two different vowels: the left one darker, the right one brighter. Between them they voice A minor, the third on one side and the fifth on the other. The keyboard’s gate opens both, and VCO A sings a line through the same vowels.

steps.title: Two drones, one chord
steps.why:
Drone 1 tuned to A1, A2, C4, A4, and Drone 4 to A1, A2, E4, C5: A minor between them. Generator 5 off on both, ATTACK 6 and RELEASE 7. PAN 1 hard left, 4 hard right, both at VOL 7. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE and Drone 4’s GATE: Drone 1 and Drone 4 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it.
- Listen for: a wide minor chord.

steps.title: Two vowels
steps.why:
Both filters to band-pass with RES 6: left FREQ 4.5 for a dark “oo”, right FREQ 5.5 for a brighter “ah”.
- Listen for: the chord sung rather than played.

steps.title: Move the vowels
steps.why:
Patch LFO A to CV L and LFO B to CV R, both slow and triangle: LFO A RATE 3, LFO B RATE 1. MOD L and MOD R 1.
- Listen for: the two vowels shifting on their own, out of step.

steps.title: A large hall
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1 (Shimmer), Z 7, BLEND 6.
- Listen for: a choir in a stone room.

steps.title: Play a line over it
steps.why:
VCO A’s VOL up to 6, WAVEFORM to triangle, Envelope A ATTACK 3, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 6. The keys play VCO A on top; the drone follows them only in time, since its pitch is set on its own knobs. Its notes overlap, so the choir holds while you play.
- Listen for: a soft melody in the drone’s key.

context.vcf.lmode: In this sound: band-pass, a single vowel-like peak.
context.lfob.rate: In this sound: 1, a slower drift than LFO A on the left.

tweaks.hear: The right vowel opens from “ah” towards “ee”.
A narrower, whistling vowel on the left.

sounds.name: Bass Under the Drone
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a bass line under a held drone
sounds.blurb: VCO B plays a slow bass line under a held A drone, with a delay to fill the space between notes.
sounds.how: The keyboard plays both VCOs at once, so turn VCO A’s channel down and VCO B carries the line alone. Its low range and SUB put it under Drone 5, which holds A and E, and the TIME cartridge’s delay answers each note.

steps.title: VCO B alone
steps.why:
VCO A’s VOL to 0, VCO B’s to 7.
- Listen for: one buzzy line.

steps.title: Down to the bass
steps.why:
VCO B’s OCTAVE to low, three octaves down, WAVEFORM to square and −1 SUB on.
- Listen for: a round, deep bass.

steps.title: Shape the notes
steps.why:
Envelope B: ATTACK 1, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 5.
- Listen for: notes that hold, then let go gently.

steps.title: The drone above
steps.why:
Drone 5, generators 1 and 2 only, tuned to A1, E2. ATTACK 6, RELEASE 8, VOL 4. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 5’s GATE: Drone 5 sounds while a key is held, so the keys (and Play) start and stop it.
- Listen for: the bass line moving against a held A.

steps.title: Warm it
steps.why:

sounds.name: Infinity Wash
sounds.ref: Classic technique: an endless reverb wash
sounds.blurb: Two drones panned apart into the INFINITY cartridge's huge resonance reverb.
sounds.how: INFINITY is the cartridge for big ambient effects; its first program is a resonance reverb whose X, Y and Z set the pre-delay, its modulation and the decay. Two classic drones, panned left and right, go through it nearly wet. The keyboard’s gate opens both drones, and VCO A plays long notes into the reverb.

steps.title: Two drones apart
steps.why:
The keys play VCO A, so this lesson turns its channel down first, to hear the drone alone.

sounds.ref: Classic technique: noise through a swept band-pass filter
sounds.blurb: Noise through two resonant band-pass filters, each swept by its own LFO: wind rising and falling.

sounds.name: Raindrops
sounds.ref: Classic technique: random sample-and-hold on a resonant filter
sounds.blurb: A resonant filter jumping to a new random pitch several times a second, ringing like drops.
sounds.how: A sample and hold grabs a random value on every tick of its clock and holds it. Patched into a resonant filter it sets the filter to a new random pitch on each tick, and the resonance rings at each one. Drone 3 makes the noise and runs its own sample and hold from its modulator; a soft noise bed underneath and a long reverb turn the drops into rain.

sounds.name: Light on the Eye
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a drone chord bent by light on its photosensor
sounds.blurb: A C major chord whose top three notes rise a fifth as light falls on the drone’s eye.
sounds.how: Each classic drone has an eye: a photosensor under a lens. Light on it raises the pitch of the generators whose MOD is on, up to an octave at full light. Here the top three of a C chord have MOD on, and the eye is lit a little over half way, which lifts them a fifth: C, E and G become C, B and D, a C major ninth. The keyboard’s gate opens the drone.

steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1 tuned to C2, G2, E3, E4, G5, ATT 6, RLS 8, VOL 7 in the middle. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE.
- Listen for: a plain C major chord, and the eye dark.

steps.why:
MOD on for generators 3, 4 and 5. Nothing changes yet: the eye is dark.
- Listen for: the same chord.

steps.title: Shine light on the eye

Drag Drone 1’s eye up to 5.8. It glows, and the three notes with MOD on rise a fifth.

steps.title: Soften it

sounds.blurb: Two drones, one each side, whose eyes blink with their own LFOs, each lifting one note of the chord.

Set the LFO to square and the eye blinks, so one note of the chord steps up and back. sounds.name: Joystick Eye

sounds.ref: Classic technique: a joystick on the filter and the effect
sounds.blurb: A saw pad where the joystick steers the filter left and right and the reverb’s size up and down.
sounds.how: A joystick moves two voltages at once with one hand. X here goes to CV L, which moves both filters through its normal to CV R; Y goes to the effector’s cv z input, which turns the CATHEDRAL’s decay. Steer right for bright, left for dark, up for a vast space and down for a close one.

steps.title: A saw pad
steps.why:
VCO A and VCO B on saw, VCO B’s TUNE 5.1, VOL 6 each, panned apart. Both envelopes: ATTACK 7, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 8, RELEASE 8.
- Listen for: a slow, wide pad.

steps.title: X on the filter
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 4, RES 3. Patch the joystick’s X out to CV L, MOD L 2, MOD R 2.
- Listen for: the pad brightening as the stick goes right.

steps.title: Y on the reverb
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1 (Shimmer), Z 3, BLEND 5. Patch the joystick’s Y out to cv z.
- Listen for: the space growing as the stick goes up.

context.joy.x: In this sound: steers the filter, right for bright.
context.joy.y: In this sound: steers the reverb, up for a longer tail.

tweaks.hear: The pad opening and closing like a slow wah.

tweaks.hear: A huge, lingering wash.

sounds.name: Polivoks Acid
sounds.ref: In the style of late-80s acid house basslines
sounds.blurb: A squelching acid line: a saw through the resonant Polivoks filter, swept by the envelope on every note and pushed into the distortion.
sounds.how: An acid line is a short, plucked saw through a resonant low-pass filter that an envelope opens on every note. The 42N has no envelope-to-filter knob, so the envelope goes in by cable: Envelope A’s env out into CV L, which reaches both filters through its normal to CV R. The 42N’s distortion after the filter, on the resonant peak, gives it the bite. Turn the glide up for slides.

steps.title: A plucked saw
steps.why:
VCO A on saw. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 5.5, SUSTAIN 1, RELEASE 2.
- Listen for: short, buzzy notes.

steps.title: Close and resonate the filter
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 3 and both RES to 8.
- Listen for: a dark, ringing tone with a whistle at the cutoff.

steps.title: Let the envelope open it
steps.why:
Patch Envelope A’s env out to CV L. MOD L and MOD R stay at 5: CV L reaches the right side through its normal.
- Listen for: each note snapping open and closing: the squelch.

steps.title: Drive it
steps.why:
DIST 5, GAIN 6, and MASTER VOLUME down to 6 for the extra level.
- Listen for: the resonant peak breaking up into a rasp.

sounds.name: Reese Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of 1990s drum & bass Reese basses
sounds.blurb: Two saws a hair apart, spread left and right with a sub underneath: the slow-churning drum & bass Reese.
sounds.how: A Reese is two sawtooths tuned almost together. They drift in and out of phase, so the bass swells and hollows as it holds. Here VCO A and VCO B play together from the keyboard, VCO B tuned a fraction sharp, and each sits on its own side, through its own filter, so the churn moves across the stereo field too. VCO A’s sub-oscillator holds the floor steady.

steps.title: Two saws
steps.why:
VCO A and VCO B on saw. VCO B VOL 7, and VCO B’s TUNE 5.25, a quarter-semitone sharp. Both envelopes: ATTACK 0, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 9, RELEASE 3.
- Listen for: a thick bass that swells and hollows slowly while a note holds.

steps.title: Spread them
steps.why:
VCO A PAN −3, VCO B PAN +3.
- Listen for: the churn moving between the speakers.

steps.title: Weight and darkness
steps.why:
VCO A’s −1 SUB on. Both FREQ to 4.5, RES 3, and MASTER VOLUME 6.
- Listen for: a round low end with the beating saws on top.

sounds.name: Wobble Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of 2010s dubstep wobble basses
sounds.blurb: A distorted saw-and-square bass whose filter LFO B swings open and shut: the dubstep wobble.
sounds.how: A wobble is an LFO on a resonant low-pass filter, fast enough to be a rhythm. LFO B, the fast one, goes into CV L, which moves both sides through its normal. The distortion after the filter turns each opening into a growl. Its rate is a knob, not a tempo, so set it by ear against the beat.

steps.title: A fat bass
steps.why:
VCO A on saw with −1 SUB on; VCO B on square, VOL 6. Envelopes: ATTACK 0, SUSTAIN 10.
- Listen for: a heavy, buzzing bass.

steps.title: Close the filter
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 3, RES 6, MOD L and MOD R to 6.
- Listen for: the bass muffled and ringing.

steps.title: Wobble it

Patch LFO B out to CV L. LFO B: rate 5.5, speed ×1, wave 0 (triangle).
- Listen for: the filter opening and shutting about two and a half times a second.

steps.title: Growl

DIST 6, GAIN 7, MASTER VOLUME 5.
- Listen for: each wobble tearing into a growl.

sounds.name: Synthwave Brass
sounds.ref: In the style of 1980s poly brass revived in synthwave
sounds.blurb: Two detuned saws that swell open with each note through a chorus: a bright 80s brass lead.
sounds.how: Synth brass is a saw whose filter opens a little behind the note, as a horn player’s lip does. Envelope A goes by cable into CV L to open both filters; its slow-ish attack gives the swell. VCO B, a few cents sharp, thickens it, and TIME’s Delay chorus program gives the 80s shimmer.

steps.title: Two saws
steps.why:
VCO A and VCO B on saw, VCO B VOL 6 and TUNE 5.1. VCO A PAN −2, VCO B PAN +2.
- Listen for: a wide, buzzing unison.

steps.title: The swell
steps.why:
Both envelopes: ATTACK 5, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 7, RELEASE 5. Both FREQ to 4, then patch Envelope A’s env out to CV L, MOD L and MOD R at 4.
- Listen for: each note blooming brighter just after it starts.

steps.title: Chorus

TIME on both sides, program 2 (Delay chorus). X 1, Y 1, Z 6, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: the brass shimmering and widening.

sounds.name: House Pluck
sounds.ref: In the style of 2010s deep-house chord plucks
sounds.blurb: A short, rounded pluck with an echo trailing it: the off-beat stab of deep house.
sounds.how: A pluck is a note that dies away quickly, its filter closing with it. Envelope A falls to nothing in a fifth of a second, and the same envelope, patched into CV L, closes the filter as it goes. A pulse wave and the sub-oscillator give it body, and TIME’s Delay reverb echoes it into the gaps.

steps.title: A pulse
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 3, and −1 SUB on.
- Listen for: a hollow, reedy tone.

steps.title: Make it pluck
steps.why:
Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 4.5, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 4.5. Both FREQ to 3.5, RES 4, and patch Envelope A’s env out to CV L.
- Listen for: a bright click that rounds off as it dies.

steps.title: Echo
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 1 (Delay reverb). X 4, Y 3, Z 3, BLEND 3.

sounds.name: Chiptune Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of 8-bit video-game music
sounds.blurb: A thin, bright pulse with the filter wide open and a quick echo: an 8-bit game tune.
sounds.how: Early game consoles made their tunes from narrow pulse waves with no filter at all. VCO A’s square, thinned with PW, and both filters turned all the way open give that bare, bright tone, and the keyboard’s octave-up button lifts it into the register game music lives in. A short TIME echo adds the bounce.

steps.title: A narrow pulse
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 2.5.
- Listen for: a thin, nasal buzz.

steps.title: No filter
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 10, RES 0.
- Listen for: the pulse bare and bright.

steps.title: Snappy and high

- Listen for: clipped, chirpy notes an octave up.

steps.title: Bounce

sounds.name: Phased Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s phased electric pianos
sounds.blurb: A soft, bell-edged tone that fades as it holds, swirling through VIBE’s phaser: 70s soul keys.
sounds.how: An electric piano note strikes and fades, never holding at full. VCO A’s sine-to-triangle morph gives a soft tone with a little edge, and VCO B adds a sine an octave down for body. The VIBE cartridge’s phaser, on both sides, sweeps notches through it slowly, as a 70s player’s phaser pedal did.

steps.title: A soft tone
steps.why:
VCO A on the sine-to-triangle morph, PW 3. VCO B on sine with its −1 SUB on, VOL 4.
- Listen for: a round tone with a quiet octave under it.

steps.title: Strike and fade
steps.why:
Both envelopes: ATTACK 0, DECAY 7, SUSTAIN 2, RELEASE 5.
- Listen for: each note striking and fading, piano-like.

steps.title: Phaser
steps.why:
VIBE on both sides, program 1 (Phaser). X 7, Y 2, BLEND 6. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: a slow swirl through the notes.

sounds.name: Dub Techno Chord
sounds.ref: In the style of 1990s Berlin dub techno chord stabs
sounds.blurb: One classic drone tuned to a minor ninth and snapped open by each key: a dub-techno chord stab, echoing into the distance.
sounds.how: Dub techno is built on one minor chord, stabbed and fed into long echoes. A classic drone is a chord machine: tune its five generators to C minor 9 and its own fast attack and short release make it a stab. The keys only open it, so every key plays the same chord, as the genre does. TIME’s delay feeds back on itself while LFO A slowly moves the filter.

steps.title: Tune a minor ninth
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1: generator 1 to C2, 2 to G2, 3 to E♭4, 4 to B♭4 and 5 to D6.
- Listen for: nothing yet: the drone is closed.

steps.title: Make it stab
steps.why:
Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE. ATT 0, RLS 3.5, and Drone 1 VOL 9, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a short, full chord on each key.

steps.title: Muffle it
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 5, RES 4. Patch LFO A out to CV L, MOD L and MOD R 2, LFO A rate 4.
- Listen for: a dark, woolly stab that brightens and darkens slowly.

steps.title: Into the echo
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 1 (Delay reverb). X 7, Y 4, Z 5, BLEND 5.
- Listen for: each stab repeating, fading and smearing into the next.

sounds.name: Drawbar Drone
sounds.ref: Classic technique: five generators tuned as an organ’s drawbars
sounds.blurb: A classic drone tuned to the harmonics an organ’s drawbars add, its MUTE buttons the stops, swirling through VIBE.
sounds.how: A drawbar organ adds pipes at the octave, the twelfth and the octaves above to one note. A classic drone’s five generators can be tuned to exactly those: C2, C3, G3, C5 and G5. Each MUTE button is then a drawbar pulled in or out, and the VIBE phaser, turned fast, stands in for the rotating speaker.

steps.title: Tune the harmonics
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 2: generator 1 to C2, 2 to C3, 3 to G3, 4 to C5, 5 to G5.
- Listen for: nothing yet: the drone is closed.

steps.title: Open it
steps.why:
Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 2’s GATE. ATT 1, RLS 4, Drone 2 PAN 0.
- Listen for: an organ-like chord on C, bright and steady.

steps.title: Pull the stops
steps.why:
Mute generators 3 and 5.
- Listen for: a plainer, flute-like organ of octaves alone.

steps.title: The rotating speaker
steps.why:
VIBE on both sides, program 1 (Phaser). X 6, Y 6, BLEND 5. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: a fast swirl, like a spinning organ speaker.

context.d2.on3: In this sound: the twelfth, the organ’s 2 ⅔′ drawbar.
context.d2.on5: In this sound: the octave-and-a-twelfth above, the brightest stop.

tweaks.hear: The fifth added: a reedier, fuller organ.

sounds.name: Pulser Gate
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a square clock chopping the filter
sounds.blurb: A held drone chord chopped into sixteenths by the pulser on the filter, with echoes filling the gaps: a trance gate.
sounds.how: A trance gate cuts a held chord into a rhythm. The 42N’s PULSER, the sequencer’s clock, is a square between −10 and +10 V. Patched into CV L it slams both filters open and shut at its speed: the chord sounds on the high half and is nearly gone on the low. The pulser keeps its own time, so set its speed against the music by ear.

steps.title: A held chord
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 4: generator 1 to A1, 2 to E2, 3 to C4, 4 to E4, 5 to B5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 4’s GATE, ATT 2, RLS 5.
- Listen for: a sustained A minor chord with a ninth on top.

steps.title: Chop it
steps.why:
Patch the pulser out to CV L. Both FREQ to 3.5, MOD L and MOD R 3, pulser 7.
- Listen for: the chord pulsing on and off five times a second.

steps.title: Fill the gaps
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 1. X 5, Y 3, Z 4, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: echoes landing between the chops.

tweaks.hear: A gentler pulse: the chord breathing, not chopped.

sounds.name: Drone Relay
sounds.ref: Classic technique: each voice’s envelope opening the next
sounds.blurb: Four classic drones in a chain, each opened by the envelope of the one before: a chord that blooms and dies voice by voice across the stereo field.
sounds.how: Every 42N drone voice has an env out, and every classic drone a GATE input, so one voice can open the next. Here the keyboard opens Drone 1; Drone 1’s envelope opens Drone 2, whose envelope opens Drone 4, whose envelope opens Drone 5. Each starts a moment after the one before it and, because each holds open while the last is still fading, ends after it too.

steps.title: The first voice
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1 is the root: generators 1 and 2 to C2 and G2, the rest muted. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 6, RLS 7, PAN −4.
- Listen for: a low fifth fading in.

steps.title: Relay to Drone 2
steps.why:
Drone 2: generator 3 to E♭4 and 4 to G4, the rest muted, ATT 6, RLS 7, PAN +4. Patch Drone 1’s env out to Drone 2’s GATE.
- Listen for: a minor third and fifth arriving on the right, just after the bass.

steps.title: Relay to Drone 4
steps.why:
Drone 4: generators 3 and 4 to B♭3 and D5, the rest muted, ATT 7, RLS 8, PAN −2. Patch Drone 2’s env out to Drone 4’s GATE.
- Listen for: the seventh and ninth joining last on the left.

steps.title: Relay to Drone 5
steps.why:
Drone 5: generator 5 alone, tuned to G6, ATT 8, RLS 9, PAN +2. Patch Drone 4’s env out to Drone 5’s GATE.
- Listen for: a high glint, the last to arrive and the last to leave.

steps.title: A room for it
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1 (Shimmer). Z 6, BLEND 5. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: the chain blooming and fading in a large space.

context.d5.rls: In this sound: how long the last voice lingers.

sounds.name: Chord Sequencer
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the sequencer lighting a drone’s eye
sounds.blurb: The sequencer steps a classic drone’s upper three generators through a progression while the bass pair holds: chords from a voice with no keyboard.
sounds.how: A classic drone has no pitch input, but its CV jack adds light to its eye, and the eye bends every generator whose MOD is on by the same amount. Put MOD on the upper three, patch the sequencer’s cv out to the CV jack, and each step moves the triad up by its own interval over a still fifth in the bass: a chord progression, planed in parallel, from one drone. The pulser clocks it and the keys open the voice.

steps.title: A triad over a fifth
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1: generator 1 to D2, 2 to A2, 3 to F3, 4 to A4, 5 to D6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 4, RLS 6, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a D minor chord, spread wide.

steps.title: Let the top three bend
steps.why:
MOD on generators 3, 4 and 5. Drone 1’s CV to 10.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet: nothing is lighting the eye.

steps.title: A progression
steps.why:
Stages 4. Step 1 at 0, step 2 at 8.3 (up five semitones), step 3 at 3.3 (up two), step 4 at 5 (up three). Pulser at 2.
- Listen for: nothing yet: the sequence is not patched.

steps.title: Light the eye
steps.why:
Patch the sequencer’s cv out to Drone 1’s CV.
- Listen for: the upper chord stepping through four positions while the bass fifth holds.

steps.title: Space
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 3 (Space reverb). X 3, Y 5, Z 6, BLEND 4. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: the steps smearing into each other.

sounds.name: Berlin School
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s Berlin-school sequencer music
sounds.blurb: The pulser runs the five-step sequencer on its own, playing VCO A and moving the filter with each step; the keys transpose it.
sounds.how: Berlin-school music is a sequence left running, changed by hand while it plays. The pulser clocks the sequencer; its cv out plays VCO A and, on a second cable, moves the filter, so higher steps are brighter. Its gate out fires Envelope A. The keyboard’s pitch still adds to VCO A, so a key changes the sequence’s key. The pulser runs on its own: this sound plays without a key held.

steps.title: Echo

sounds.name: Random Computer
sounds.ref: Classic technique: sample and hold on the pitch
sounds.blurb: Every key plays a new, random pitch near it: a Papa Srapa’s sample and hold, clocked by the keys, scattering VCO A like a 70s film computer.
sounds.how: Each Papa Srapa voice has a sample and hold of white noise: on each clock it grabs the noise’s voltage and holds it. Clocked by the keyboard’s gate and patched into VCO A’s cv, it throws each note to a random pitch, as far as CV AMT lets it. The Papa Srapa itself stays silent; only its sample and hold is used. MAGIC’s pitch delay echoes each blip an octave up.

steps.title: A blip
steps.why:
VCO A on triangle. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3.
- Listen for: short, soft blips, all on the same note.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold
steps.why:
Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 3’s S&H clock, and Drone 3’s S&H out to VCO A’s cv. CV AMT 4.
- Listen for: each blip landing on a new, random pitch.

steps.title: Echoes an octave up

MAGIC on both sides, program 1 (Pitch delay). X 4, Y 5, Z 10, BLEND 4. Both FREQ to 8.
- Listen for: each blip answered by a higher, chirping echo.

sounds.name: The Drone Listens
sounds.ref: Classic technique: an envelope follower on an internal voice
sounds.blurb: VCO A is silent in the mix but feeds the envelope follower, so the rhythm you play opens a band-pass filter on a drone chord: the drone speaks in your rhythm.
sounds.how: The envelope follower turns the loudness of whatever reaches the preamp into a voltage. Nothing says that has to come from outside: patch VCO A’s dry out into the PREAMP’s ext. source and turn VCO A’s mixer channel down. Each note you play is then heard only as the follower’s voltage, opening the filter on a drone chord. Short, plucked notes give short, vocal openings; held notes hold it open.

steps.title: A drone chord
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1: generator 1 to E2, 2 to B2, 3 to G3, 4 to D5, 5 to F♯6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE, ATT 3, RLS 8, VOL 9, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a dense E minor chord.

steps.title: A narrow band
steps.why:
Both filters BP, FREQ 3, RES 6.
- Listen for: the chord thin and muffled.

steps.title: Feed VCO A to the follower
steps.why:
Patch VCO A’s dry out to the PREAMP’s ext. source. PREAMP gain 7; its mixer VOL stays 0. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 4, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3.
- Listen for: nothing new: VCO A is heard by the follower alone.

steps.title: Let it open the filter
steps.why:
Patch the envelope follower’s env out to CV L. MOD L and MOD R 4.
- Listen for: the chord opening in a vowel-like “wah” on each note you play.

steps.title: Room
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1. Z 4, BLEND 3.
- Listen for: the “wah” ringing on in the space.

context.pre.gain: In this sound: how hard VCO A pushes the follower.

sounds.name: Filter FM Growl
sounds.ref: Classic technique: an oscillator modulating the filter at audio rate
sounds.blurb: VCO B, unheard, shakes the filter on a drone at audio rate, so the keys change the drone’s growl rather than its pitch.
sounds.how: VCO B’s osc output is its oscillator before its envelope: it runs all the time. Patched into CV L, it moves the cutoff hundreds of times a second, which adds new, clangorous partials to whatever goes through the filter. The keys set VCO B’s pitch, and so which partials appear, while the drone underneath keeps its own pitch.

steps.title: A low drone
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 4: generators 1 and 2 to C2 and G2, generator 3 to C4, 4 and 5 muted. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE, ATT 2, RLS 5, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a plain low fifth with an octave.

steps.title: A resonant filter
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 5, RES 5.
- Listen for: the drone a little hollow.

sounds.name: Night Insects
sounds.ref: Classic technique: two Papa Srapa voices chirping at different rates
sounds.blurb: Both Papa Srapa voices, high and chopped at different speeds, one each side: crickets and tree frogs on a warm night.
sounds.how: A Papa Srapa’s AM switches its tone on and off at the modulator’s rate; FM adds a trill. At high pitch and fast rates that is an insect. The two Papa Srapa voices run at unrelated rates, so their chirps never line up, and each sits on its own side. A reverb puts them outdoors.

- Listen for: a fast, buzzing chirr on the left.

steps.why:

- Listen for: a slower, lower chirp on the right that never falls in step.

steps.title: Outdoors
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 3 (Space reverb). X 2, Y 4, Z 5, BLEND 4. Both FREQ to 8.
- Listen for: the chirps carrying into a wide, open space.

sounds.name: Laser Battle
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a voice’s envelope sweeping its own pitch
sounds.blurb: A Papa Srapa’s own envelope, patched back into its pitch, makes every key a falling laser zap, thrown backwards by MAGIC’s reverse pitch delay.
sounds.how: A Papa Srapa’s env out is its own envelope, 0 to +8 V, and its cv input moves its pitch by octaves. Patched from one to the other, the tone leaps up as the voice opens and falls as it closes: with a fast attack and a quick release, a zap. MAGIC’s second program reverses and drops its echoes, so the zaps ricochet.

sounds.name: Resonator Pings
sounds.ref: Classic technique: noise bursts exciting a feedback delay
sounds.blurb: Short bursts of Papa Srapa noise ring a very short, feeding-back delay into metallic, pitched pings.
sounds.how: A delay of a few milliseconds fed back on itself rings at the pitch its length sets: a comb filter, the trick behind plucked-string models. INFINITY’s third program, Resonance delay, is one, with Y setting the length (so the pitch) and Z shifting the pitch of each pass, so the ring spirals. Short bursts of noise from a Papa Srapa strike it.

steps.title: Bursts of noise
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 3: NOISE 10, ATT 0, RLS 1.5, VOL 10, PAN 0. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. MASTER VOLUME 9.
- Listen for: short ticks of white noise.

- Listen for: each tick ringing into a pitched, metallic ping.

sounds.name: Warped Tape
sounds.ref: Classic technique: an LFO on a delay’s time
sounds.blurb: A soft melody whose echoes bend in pitch as LFO A stretches INFINITY’s O.D.D. delay: a worn, warped tape.
sounds.how: Changing a delay’s time while it holds sound bends the pitch of what is in it, as a stretched tape does. The effector’s cv inputs move X, Y and Z by voltage; LFO A into cv y slowly sweeps the O.D.D. program’s delay time, so the repeats drift sharp and flat while the dry melody stays in tune.

sounds.name: Two Sides
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a different path on each side
sounds.blurb: VCO A goes left through a band-pass filter and a flanger, VCO B right through a low-pass and a shimmer reverb: one melody in two different rooms.
sounds.how: The 42N’s left and right are two separate paths: each has its own filter, with its own BP / LP button, and its own cartridge program. Pan a voice hard to one side and it takes that side’s path alone. Here the same melody, played by both VCOs a fourth apart, sounds thin and swirling on the left and full and glowing on the right. X, Y and Z are shared, so each knob turns a different thing on each side.

sounds.name: Envelope Polyrhythm
sounds.ref: Classic technique: two looping envelopes at different speeds
sounds.blurb: Both VCO envelopes loop, at speeds that do not divide into each other, so every held note becomes two pulses, one each side, falling in and out of step.
sounds.how: With LOOP on, a 42N envelope cycles its attack and decay for as long as it is open: the VCO pulses on its own. Give VCO A and VCO B different speeds and the two pulse trains drift against each other, a rhythm neither plays alone. The keys set the pitch and how long it runs.

sounds.name: Drone Metal
sounds.ref: In the style of 2000s drone metal
sounds.blurb: Two classic drones tuned to a low D power chord, slowly swelling into the distortion at full: a wall of amplified sound.
sounds.how: Drone metal holds one detuned, distorted power chord for minutes. Two classic drones give the low fifths, each generator slightly off the next, so the chord churns. The 42N’s distortion after the filter, all the way in, saturates them like an amplifier, and a big reverb gives the room.

steps.title: Open them slowly
steps.why:

- Listen for: a low, buzzing power chord swelling in.

- Listen for: the chord saturating into a roaring wall.

sounds.name: Joystick Bend
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a joystick on the pitch and the vibrato
sounds.blurb: A sine lead where the joystick bends the pitch left and right and deepens a delay vibrato up and down: a hand-played, theremin-like voice.
sounds.how: The joystick’s X and Y outs are two voltages from one hand. X goes into VCO A’s cv, where CV AMT keeps it to about an octave either way: the stick bends the note. Y goes into the effector’s cv z, which on TIME’s third program, Delay vibrato, is the vibrato’s depth. Add portamento and the keys glide too.

sounds.name: Octave Ghosts
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a Papa Srapa played from the keys
sounds.blurb: A Papa Srapa’s square tone played from the keyboard, each note answered by ghostly echoes an octave up from MAGIC’s Bell pitch delay.
sounds.how: A Papa Srapa voice has no keyboard of its own, but its cv input moves its pitch an octave a volt, and the keyboard’s v/oct out is exactly that. With its PITCH set to C4, the keys play it in tune. MAGIC’s Bell pitch delay sends each note back an octave higher, and Z shifts the repeats up another octave, so they climb as they fade.

sounds.name: Shortwave
sounds.ref: Classic technique: noise, AM and a swept band-pass as a radio
sounds.blurb: A crackling, warbling radio between stations: Papa Srapa noise and a chopped tone through a slowly swept band-pass, a hum underneath.
sounds.how: Tuning a shortwave radio passes static, whistling carriers and chopped signals. Drone 3 makes the signal: a high tone chopped fast by AM and warbled by FM, with noise blended in. Drone 6 is the mains hum, low and plain. A band-pass filter swept by LFO A is the tuning dial, passing first one and then another.

- Listen for: a low hum under the static.

- Listen for: the band sweeping slowly up and down, picking out the whistle, the static and the hum in turn.

sounds.name: Sunrise
sounds.ref: Classic technique: all eight voices at once
sounds.blurb: Every voice of the 42N at once: four classic drones rising as a chord, a Papa Srapa’s surf, the other’s birds, and both VCOs singing over the top.
sounds.how: The 42N is eight voices in one box, and this sound uses all of them. Four classic drones spread a chord across the stereo field, each opening slowly. Drone 3 is low, filtered surf; Drone 6 high, chopped birdsong. VCO A plays the melody and VCO B a softer line a fourth below. One keyboard gate opens every drone; the keys play the VCOs.

steps.title: The chord
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0 for now. Drone 1: C2, G2, E3, C5, G5. Drone 2: generator 1 muted, then C3, G3, E4, C6. Both ATT 7, RLS 8, VOL 4. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to each one’s GATE.
- Listen for: a wide C major chord rising slowly.

steps.title: Widen it
steps.why:
Drone 4: A1, E2, D4, A4, generator 5 muted. Drone 5: only generators 4 and 5, B4 and E6. ATT 8, RLS 9, VOL 3, PANs −4 and +4. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to each.
- Listen for: the chord spreading wider with a sixth and a ninth.

Drone 3: NOISE 10, ATT 8, RLS 8, VOL 3. Drone 6: HI on, PITCH 9, AM on, FM on, MOD 3, rate 6, ATT 5, RLS 6, VOL 2. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to both.
- Listen for: a hiss of surf beneath and chirps high above.

VCO A on sine-to-triangle, VOL 5. VCO B on triangle, TUNE 0.83 (a fourth below), VOL 3. Both envelopes: ATTACK 3, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 7, RELEASE 6.
- Listen for: a soft melody in fourths floating over everything.

VCO A on sine with its sub-oscillator gives the depth; PORTAMENTO makes every new note glide from the last; a touch of the distortion after the filter adds the growl that lets it cut through on small speakers.

sounds.name: Breathy Flute
sounds.ref: In the style of synthesised flutes in 70s library music
sounds.blurb: A soft sine flute with real breath: a Papa Srapa’s noise opened by the same keys, so every note starts with a puff of air.
sounds.how: A flute is a near-sine with breath noise on its attack. VCO A gives the tone with a slow-ish attack; Drone 3, turned to noise alone and opened by the keyboard’s gate with a quick release, adds the breath. A gentle vibrato from LFO B on VCO A’s cv brings it to life.

steps.why:

sounds.name: Endless Oscillator
sounds.ref: Classic technique: an oscillator patched past its envelope

sounds.how: VCO B’s osc out is the oscillator itself, before its envelope and VCA. Patched into EXT. AUDIO in, it reaches the mixer on a channel of its own that no key opens or closes: it sounds all the time, at the pitch of the last key. Portamento makes it glide from one to the next, under VCO A playing as usual.

sounds.name: Modulator Sync
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a Papa Srapa’s modulator syncing a VCO

sounds.how: Sync restarts an oscillator each time a signal rises. The usual master is the other VCO, but any square will do: a Papa Srapa’s modulator out is one, from slow to buzzing. Synced to it, VCO A sounds at the modulator’s rate, a low buzz, while VCO A’s own pitch, from the keys, decides the tone inside each cycle: the keys play colour, not notes.

sounds.name: Wandering Chords

sounds.how: A Papa Srapa’s S&H, with nothing in its clock, is clocked by its own modulator, so it hands out a new random voltage at the modulator’s rate even while the voice is silent. Into a classic drone’s CV it moves the light on the eye up and down from where the LIGHT knob leaves it, and the generators whose MOD is on jump with it: a chord that keeps wandering.

sounds.name: Glitch Echo

sounds.how: Jumping a delay’s time while it holds sound makes its repeats skip and bend. The effector’s cv y moves Y, which on TIME is the delay time; a Papa Srapa’s sample and hold gives it a new random length at its modulator’s rate. The dry melody stays clean while its echoes glitch.

sounds.name: Pulse-Width FM
sounds.ref: Classic technique: an oscillator modulating another’s pulse width
sounds.blurb: VCO B, unheard, moves VCO A’s pulse width at audio rate: a reedy, ring-modulated tone that changes character as VCO B is retuned.
sounds.how: Pulse-width modulation is usually slow. At audio rate it becomes a kind of FM: the width changes hundreds of times a cycle, adding sidebands. VCO B’s osc out into VCO A’s pwm input does that; both follow the keys, so the sound stays in tune, and VCO B’s TUNE picks the colour.

sounds.name: Metal Scrape

Only the generators whose MOD is on rise with it, so the drone’s top swoops while its bottom holds.

sounds.name: Pumping Pad
sounds.ref: Classic technique: one side’s loudness opening the other’s filter
sounds.blurb: A Papa Srapa thump on the right feeds the envelope follower, which opens the left side’s filter on a drone pad: a pad that pulses in time with the beat.
sounds.how: WET OUT R is a signal like any other, so it can feed the PREAMP and the envelope follower. Put a rhythm on the right and a pad on the left, and the follower’s voltage into CV L opens the left filter on every beat. MOD R at 0 keeps the right side out of it, though CV L still reaches it through the normal.

sounds.name: Wobble That Follows
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a sub-audio VCO as a key-tracked LFO
sounds.blurb: VCO B, dropped to OCT LOW and unheard, wobbles the filter at a rate set by the key you play: high notes wobble fast, low notes slow.
sounds.how: An LFO has its own rate, but a VCO follows the keys. VCO B at OCT LOW runs three octaves under the key, which for bass notes is slow enough to hear as a wobble, not a pitch. Patched into CV L, it moves the filter on VCO A’s bass at a rate that rises an octave for every octave you play: an LFO that tracks the keyboard.

sounds.name: Stepping Echoes
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the sequencer moving a pitch delay
sounds.blurb: The sequencer steps MAGIC’s pitch delay to a new interval every beat, so each held note’s echoes climb a different chord.
sounds.how: The effector’s cv z moves Z, which on MAGIC’s pitch delay sets how far each echo is shifted. The sequencer’s cv out there makes the shift step: an echo a fourth up, then a fifth, then an octave. Run by the pulser, it keeps changing the harmony of the echoes while you play.

steps.title: A bell tone
steps.why:
VCO A on the sine-to-triangle morph, PW 5. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 7, SUSTAIN 3, RELEASE 6.
- Listen for: a soft, bell-like melody.

steps.title: A pitch delay
steps.why:
MAGIC on both sides, program 1 (Pitch delay). X 6, Y 5, Z 5, BLEND 5.
- Listen for: echoes at the same pitch.

steps.title: Step the shift
steps.why:
Patch the sequencer’s cv out to the effector’s cv z. Stages 4: steps 0, 4.17, 5.83, 10 (unison, a fourth, a fifth, an octave). Pulser 3.
- Listen for: the echoes shifting to a new interval about once a second.

context.seq.s4: In this sound: the octave step: 1.2 semitones of shift per division.

tweaks.hear: Echoes skittering between intervals.
Echoes of echoes, each shifted again: rising arpeggios.

sounds.name: Rhythm Section
sounds.ref: Classic technique: one modulator clocking the sequencer and a hi-hat
sounds.blurb: Drone 3’s modulator clocks the sequencer and chops Drone 3’s own noise, so a ticking hi-hat and a sequenced bass run off the same clock: a self-playing groove.
sounds.how: A Papa Srapa’s modulator out is a square clock. Patched to the sequencer’s clock in, it steps the bass line; the same modulator chops Drone 3’s noise with AM, a hi-hat ticking at exactly the same rate. Two parts, one clock, always in time. Both run on their own, with the hi-hat on HOLD, so the groove plays without a key held; a short tap on a key transposes the bass.

steps.title: A sequenced bass
steps.why:
VCO A on saw, −1 SUB on. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3. Both FREQ to 4.5, RES 5. Steps 0, 0, 1.17, 2, 1.67.
- Listen for: nothing yet: nothing gates or clocks it.

steps.title: Drone 3 is the clock
steps.why:
Drone 3’s rate 7.4. Patch its modulator out to the sequencer’s clock in; the sequencer’s cv out to VCO A’s 1v/oct and gate out to Envelope A’s gate.
- Listen for: the bass line stepping about three times a second.

steps.title: The hi-hat
steps.why:
Drone 3: NOISE 10, AM on, HOLD on, VOL 3, PAN +3.
- Listen for: a ticking hiss locked to the bass.

steps.title: Room
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 1. X 3, Y 3, Z 3, BLEND 2.
- Listen for: a short echo around the groove.

context.d3.rate: In this sound: the tempo of both parts at once.

tweaks.hear: The whole groove slowing together.
A shorter, tumbling bass figure.

sounds.name: Robot Chatter
sounds.ref: Classic technique: one Papa Srapa’s sample and hold on the other’s pitch
sounds.blurb: Drone 6’s sample and hold throws Drone 3’s pitch to a new random note many times a second: the beeping, burbling chatter of a film robot.
sounds.how: Each Papa Srapa has a sample and hold, clocked by its own modulator. Drone 6’s, running fast, sends a new random voltage to Drone 3’s pitch several times a second, and Drone 3 jumps with it: a stream of random beeps. Drone 3’s own AM, at another rate, breaks the stream into phrases.

steps.title: A high beep
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 3: HI on, PITCH 5.5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE, ATT 0, RLS 2, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a plain square beep on each key.

steps.title: Random notes
steps.why:
Patch Drone 6’s S&H out to Drone 3’s cv. Drone 6: 1 / 10 on, rate 5.
- Listen for: the beep jumping to a new random note many times a second.

steps.title: Phrases
steps.why:
Drone 3: AM on, rate 5.
- Listen for: the chatter breaking into bursts, like speech.

steps.title: Tame it
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 6.5. TIME on both sides, program 1. X 3, Y 2, Z 2, BLEND 2.
- Listen for: softer chatter with a little room.

Each beep trilling.
